title: Types, variables, operators and string formatting

videos.script:
There is a question you have to be able to answer about every value in every program you ever write, and it is not what the value is. It is what KIND of thing it is. {{kind}}

Here is why that matters in the first minute. Two plus two is four. But quote two, quote two, and add them — and the honest answer is twenty-two. {{twentytwo}} Not a bug. Not the language being clever. Those are two different kinds of thing, and plus means something different for each of them. For numbers it adds. For text it joins.

{{decides}} That is the idea the whole lesson is built on: the type decides what the operator means. Not the operator, not you — the type.

Python does not make you say which kind a value is. You write it down and the interpreter works it out. That is comfortable and it is also why the first `TypeError` surprises people: nobody told them there were types, so the message arrives about a thing they did not know existed.

{{today}} Today: the kinds you will use every day. Whole numbers with no upper limit. Decimals that cannot hold a third exactly. Text, which is immutable, and the dozen methods that do most of the work with it. True and False, and the surprising set of things that count as false. And `None`, which is the value that means there is no value.

{{fstring}} Plus the one piece of syntax you will type more than any other in this course. An f-string — an f, a quote, and braces where the values go. It is the reason nobody writes plus signs between pieces of text any more, and once you have it you will not go back.

Four values and four operators, and I am going to pair them up wrongly on purpose to see what each mistake sounds like.

{{setup}} Here are my four: the integer 2, the float 2.0, the string "2", and the list containing 2.

{{plus}} Integer plus integer — four. Float plus integer — 4.0, and note that the float wins; anything touching a float comes back a float. String plus string — "22", joined. And string plus integer — there it is. TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str. Read it: it names both kinds, and it tells you which one it was willing to accept.

{{star}} Now multiply. Two times three, six. But string times three — "222". Multiplication on text means repeat. That is not a trick, it is the same rule: the type decides what the operator means.

{{divide}} Divide two by one and you get 2.0, a float, even though both sides were whole. Python's division always produces a float. If you want the whole part, that is two slashes.

{{compare}} And comparison. "2" equals 2 is False — not an error, False. Different kinds, so they are not the same value. That one is worth sitting with, because it is a comparison that silently answers no and never raises anything for you to read.

{{lesson}} Four pairings, one error, one surprise and one silent no. The error you will fix in seconds. The silent no is the one that costs an afternoon, and it comes from exactly this: forgetting that what came back from `input` is text.

Three things to keep.

{{one}} The type decides what the operator means. Plus joins text and adds numbers. Times repeats text and multiplies numbers. When something behaves strangely, `type()` is the first question, and it answers instantly.

{{two}} Floats cannot hold every decimal. Nought point one plus nought point two is not nought point three, in every language on every machine, and it is arithmetic rather than a defect. For money, lesson 7 has `Decimal`. For a comparison, never `==` on two floats.

{{three}} And f-strings. An f before the quote, braces around anything you want printed, and a colon inside the braces when you want to say how. Two decimal places, a thousands separator, a fixed width. You will type this more than any other syntax in the course.

{{next}} Next lesson is the four containers — list, tuple, dictionary and set — and the question each of them answers. That is where programs stop being about one value at a time.
